title: Type I-II/II-I vortices from dimension-six self-interaction
authors: A. Alonso-Izquierdo, A. González-Parra, K. Slawinska, A. Wereszczynski, T. Winyard
abstract: We show that adding a dimension-six self-interaction to the Abelian-Higgs or Ginzburg Landau model results in a remarkable and rich structure of multi-vortex solutions. Besides the standard type I (attractive) and type II (repulsive) regimes, separated by the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfeld limit (BPS), we identify two new possibilities: type I-II vortices, which attract at short distances and repel at long distances; and type II-I vortices, with the opposite behaviour. Specifically, within the type II-I regime, multi-vortex solutions form chunks of the Abrikosov lattice or clusters. Conversely, in the I-II regime, axially symmetric multi-vortices are stable; nevertheless, depending on the model parameters and topological charge (winding number), they can be either the ground state or not.
summary: This work investigates how adding a dimension-six self-interaction term modifies the vortex structure in Abelian-Higgs models. It reveals the existence of novel mixed-type vortices (I-II and II-I) that exhibit alternating short- and long-range forces. This theoretical finding expands the understanding of vortex physics beyond the standard Type I/II classification, suggesting new stable configurations in superconductors and related field theories.
main_problem: To characterize the complex multi-vortex solutions that arise when a dimension-six self-interaction term is added to the standard Abelian-Higgs or Ginzburg-Landau model.
main_result: The model supports four distinct vortex regimes (Type I, II, I-II, II-I), with the latter two exhibiting mixed short-range attraction/long-range repulsion or vice versa. These mixed types allow for stable, structured vortex arrangements like Abrikosov lattice chunks.
method: The analysis combines asymptotic solutions for long-range forces, spectral analysis of the vortex core to determine short-range forces, and numerical minimization of the energy functional.
model_or_system: The system is described by a modified Abelian-Higgs model in 2+1 dimensions, featuring a potential $V$ that includes a sextic self-interaction term, extending the standard quartic Higgs potential.
key_observables: Long-range interaction energy $E_{	ext{int}}(d)$, short-range force (determined by spectral modes), and the binding energy ratio $E_N / (N E_1)$ for multi-vortex states.
important_parameters: The coupling constants $\lambda$ and $b$ govern the transition between the different vortex types, with the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfeld (BPS) limit marking a key boundary.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on asymptotic expansions for long-range behavior and heuristic arguments near the vortex core, though the results suggest the mixed types are robust features of the theory.
figures_summary: Figure 1 maps the phase structure in the $(\lambda, b)$ plane showing the four vortex regimes. Figures 2 and 3 provide examples of Type II-I solutions forming lattice chunks or clusters. Figure 4 illustrates the transition of binding energy minima for Type I-II solutions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the force regimes (long-range vs. short-range) dictated by the parameters $\lambda$ and $b$, mapping out the phase diagram of vortex types, and then examines the stability and structure of multi-vortex configurations within these identified regimes.
why_interesting: The discovery of stable, mixed-type vortices (I-II and II-I) demonstrates how adding higher-order interaction terms can fundamentally alter the topological stability and interaction physics of condensed matter systems, which is relevant to understanding complex superconducting or magnetic phase transitions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Structure of the phases of the vortex solutions. Type I: short and long-range attraction. Type II: short and long-range repulsion. Type I-II: short-range attraction and long-range repulsion. Type II-I: short-range repulsion and long-range attraction. The black dot represents the BPS limit λ = 1 and b = 0. The dashed and dotted-dashed lines correspond to the curves that separate long-range attraction from repulsion, eq. (13). The solid line represents the positive/negative mode separatrix, eq. (14). The dotted line is its analytical approximation.

Figure 4: The binding energies EN/(NE1), where the subscript is the winding number, of coincident zero solutions for type I-II solutions for b = 2.0. For small/large λ higher N solutions are always/never global minimisers. However, nearer critical coupling, there is a critical value of winding Nλ,b for which N < Nλ,b the coincident zero solution is only local which for N ≥Nλ,b it is the global minimiser.
Figure 2: The type II-I regime. Example of the solutions being chunks of the Abrikosov lattice. We plot the local magnetic field strength B of bound states for λ = 1.6, b = −1.2.
Figure 3: The type II-I regime. Example of solutions with larger optimal separation clustering. We plot the local magnetic field strength B of bound states for λ = 0.5, b = −1.6.
